title: Don Brown, the Blackfoot arranger, and his later life
summary: He tells how Don Brown copied Lunceford's Frisco Fog by ear and of his decline.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah, we took the Indian, the one that I told you about, the Blackfoot, Don Brown... I got him in the band over in Seattle. We had a band over there. I got him to come over to Seattle. He wasn't doing anything. He was in Butte or something like that, playing some joint. And I got him to come over to Seattle. And we bought him a jug ..(?).. Lunceford's record of "Frisco Fog," which is a tough arrangement, very complicated. And we bought Don this jug and went up to the hotel room, opened up the jug, got the score paper out... Well, the score paper didn't make anything, just parts. And he just started, and he started with a... I don't know how he started. He'd usually start with a guitar part or something like that. And he copied the whole arrangement that afternoon, note-for-note, perfect. And then it took us about three weeks before we could play it. But he could do that easy. He'd hear exactly where that third alto player was going, or the fourth or like that.
Well, when he got out of the Service... They

drafted him. And when he got out of the Service, he went with... He started writing. He wrote some stuff for Jimmy Dorsey, and he was around Hollywood for a while, but he couldn't stand the Hollywood people. He was like an outlaw. He was born a hundred years too late. He should have been born when they were fighting, because he loved to fight -- and boy, he could fight. I saw him take six guys one night, six, in about three minutes. Wiped 'em out. That's an accomplishment. All he got was a black eye.
He didn't like... He used to write me letters telling me how much he hated Hollywood.

Then he went with Sonny Dunham, and he'd drink... And there ain't nothin' worse than a drunken Indian, especially when they're full of blood. He'd fall off the stand... They finally just left him layin' there one night and took off. And then he started hittin' the Army hospitals. He was getting a pension from the Government for being an Indian; you get so much a month, $300 or something like that. And then his...

...Veterans... And as soon as they'd think he was in pretty good shape, they'd turn him loose and give him all this bread. First thing he'd do was, he'd go down to a clothing store, like Sy Devore(?) or something, buy himself

some real sharp clothes, and head for Main Street, the worst part of town, and start spending his money and buying people drinks and getting drunk -- and the first thing you know, he'd wind up...he'd be in jail. And they'd take all his clothes. He'd wake up with another pair of shoes on, and this and that. Fortunately, his brother was in town; his brother was a CPA. He called him and he'd come down and bail him out, take him back out to the hospital and start him all over again.
